As of 2024, bike counts grew twice as fast as the bike network. Locations with separated bike lanes—
Cambridge St, Garden St, Hampshire St, Massachusetts Ave—saw the greatest growth in biking. Similarly,
locations with physical separation—separated bike lanes or paths—saw the greatest growth in children biking.
Separated bike lanes are the fastest-growing part of the Cambridge bike network. Click here to learn more.

As of 2024, the citywide annual bike crash rate has declined 41% since 2004. Bike crashes were lower in the
most recent five-year period compared to pre-pandemic levels, though annual bike crash numbers have
increased from the historic lows observed during the COVID-19 pandemic. While the number of bike crashes
that resulted in injury also declined during this most recent five-year period, most bike crashes are still injury
crashes. Click here to learn more.

The Cambridge Water Department quantifies how many people walk and bike at Fresh Pond Reservation
through its Census Program. Today, the Census Program collects data at six trail locations. Between 2015 and
2024, this program included a seventh location at the Fresh Pond Bike Path. Between 2021 and 2023, biking at
this location more than doubled from about 66,500 bike counts to 142,300 (see Figure 9). The Watertown-

explains why bike counts increased so significantly.
Though the Fresh Pond Bike Path counter was decommissioned in 2024, the Census Program continues to
collect bike counts at a nearby, separate counter at Perimeter Rd. This location has seen increased bike counts
since 2022, though on a much smaller scale compared to the Fresh Pond Bike Path Counter (see Figure 9).

Customer intercept surveys, conducted as part of Commerial District Assessments, found that 15% to 30% of
visitors to the City’s commercial districts arrived by bike (see Figure 11). All commercial districts have seen an
increase in the proportion of people arriving by bike except Harvard Square, which remained at 15% between
2016 and 2022. The most recent round of customer intercept surveys found that the East Cambridge
Commercial District had the most people using bikes for transportation (30% of visitors). It also saw the
biggest increase in biking, with the rate going up by 19 percentage points. Surveys happen in a different
commercial district each year in the spring or fall. Surveys rely on voluntary responses from people on
sidewalks and in plazas.

How has Cambridge’s bike network evolved ov er time?

The bike netwo hraks grown steadi slyince 2004.
The City, State, and partners have greatly increased bikeway lane-miles over the past several decades. Total
lane-miles of bikeways have more than doubled between 2004 and 2024, creating a more connected and
accessible bike network (see Figure 21). As shown in the figure, biking has grown significantly at the same
time. Readers can view the evolution of the bike network in the Citywide Bicycle Count Data portal by first
selecting “Data Viewer” and then the “Map” tab.
The bike network is becoming more comfortable for people of all ages .a nd abilitie
Physically separated bikeways, like separated bike lanes and shared-use paths, appeal to people of all ages,
abilities, and identities. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology pioneered separated bike lanes in 2003
with the reconstruction of Vassar St. Since 2017 with the completion of the Cambridge Street Bicycle Safety
Demonstration Project, the City has invested in separated bike lanes and, as a result, this type of bikeway
continues to make up an increasingly larger share of total bike network lane-miles (see Figure 21). At the same
time, standard bike lanes are playing a smaller role in the bike network and their lane-miles peaked in 2019.
That’s because many separated bike lane projects, for example Hampshire St, replaced standard bike lanes.

The Garden Street Safety Improvement Project, completed fall 2022, installed 1.25 miles of quick-build
separated bike lanes between Huron Ave and Mason St. This project is unique compared to other safety
improvement projects. In 2022, the project changed Garden St to one-way operation for vehicles between
Huron Ave and Concord Ave to preserve some on-street parking. In April 2025, the City Council approved a
Policy Order instructing the City to convert Garden St back to two-way operation for vehicles while keeping the
separated bike lanes. This change will result in a two-way separated bike lane on the south side of Garden St
and the elimination of most of the existing street parking. The City anticipates these changes will occur in the
summer of 2026. Since 2024, ongoing utility work resulted in removed flex-posts and poor pavement quality,
making this route less appealing.

Has the citywide bike crash rate changed ove r time?

Yes, the bike crash rate has steadily declined since 2004 but resmtaabilne seidn ce the
COVID-19 Pandem. ic
The citywide annual bike crash rate declined from about 21 to 12 bike crashes per million BMT in 2004 and
2024, respectively (see Figure 27). That’s because estimated BMT has increased while reported bike crashes
have decreased (see Figure 28). Estimated BMT increased 233% since 2004, growing from 3.7 million miles
traveled to 12.8 million miles traveled in 2024. Reported bike crashes peaked in 2012, then dropped in the
years leading up to the COVID-19 pandemic. Although reported bike crashes have increased since the COVID-
19 pandemic, they remain below pre-pandemic peaks. This has resulted in more stable bike crash rates in
recent years despite continued growth of the estimated BMT.
